title: Short Stuff: Divorcing Your Parents
summary: Short Stuff episode on divorcing your parents, meaning legal emancipation of a minor. The hosts explain that emancipation lets a minor act as an adult in many respects (sign contracts, keep earnings, live independently, sue or be sued, choose a school), while still being barred from dropping out of school without pursuing a GED and from marrying without parental consent in most cases. They cover age of majority differences by state (California is very low, most states about sixteen, some eighteen), why child actors in Hollywood often emancipate, and the contrasting case of a child in an abusive home who must go to court, where parents are notified and can contest, a guardian ad litem may be appointed, and judges weigh reasons, maturity, health and ability to self-support. They note child labor laws still apply to emancipated kids and close on how sad the topic is.

segments.title: Opening banter and Reconcilable Differences
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short episode on divorcing your parents, joking about the 1996 movie Reconcilable Differences with Drew Barrymore and the Cheers cast.

segments.title: What emancipation means and age of majority by state
segments.summary: Legal emancipation is the process by which a minor steps forward to become legally independent of parents. The age of majority varies by state: California is very low, most states around sixteen, and some eighteen. Parents have legal duties to care for children, which is the bargain a minor seeks to escape.

segments.title: Hollywood child actors and emancipation
segments.summary: Emancipation is common among child actors in California's movie industry, often to make career matters easier and to protect earnings from parents' control. Some kid actors from other states emancipate and live alone.

segments.title: Rights gained and limits after emancipation
segments.summary: An emancipated minor can sign contracts, work and keep earnings, rent an apartment, sue or be sued, and choose a school. They still cannot drop out of school unless pursuing a GED, and cannot marry without parental consent unless pregnant or already a parent in many states.

segments.title: Emancipation in cases of abuse and the court process
segments.summary: Kids in abusive or neglectful homes face a contested court process, unlike the quick process in California. Parents must be notified and can contest. Minors cannot seek relief alone in most states, so a guardian ad litem is assigned. Judges weigh neglect, abuse, abandonment, age, maturity, health and ability to self-support.

segments.title: Child labor laws and the cost to childhood
segments.summary: Emancipated minors still fall under child labor laws and must still get schooling. Hosts reflect that emancipation may be a child's only escape, at the cost of childhood, and that the topic becomes depressing on closer look.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the short episode, noting they are bummed out, and close with the show's production credit.
